content: The incidence and prevalence of healthcare-associated infections (HAIs), including those caused by antimicrobial-resistant microorganisms, were evaluated. Secondary outcomes such as hand hygiene compliance, alcohol-based hand rub consumption, and healthcare workers’ knowledge were also assessed. Further details are available in the web appendices I and II. Evidence identification and retrieval followed the WHO Guidelines Development Plan, approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. The primary source of evidence was a systematic review conducted by the “Systematic review and evidence-based guidance on organization of hospital infection control programmes” (SIGHT) group, sponsored by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. This review spanned from 1996 to 2012 and identified ten key components of infection prevention and control (IPC) programs at the facility level. The review was updated by the WHO IPC Global Unit between November 2015 and March 2016. Concurrently, another systematic review focusing on the national level was commissioned to the Safeguarding Health through Infection Prevention research group at Glasgow Caledonian University, United Kingdom. Additionally, an inventory report of existing national and regional strategic documents and action plans was developed by the WHO IPC Global Unit team, based on a repository from a previous survey and an online survey. The SIGHT review and its update were used to evaluate the effectiveness of key components of IPC programs at the facility level. The SIGHT review was reported according to PRISMA guidelines by three participating institutions: University of Geneva Hospitals (Switzerland), Imperial College London (United Kingdom), and the University Hospital of Freiburg (Germany). Databases searched included Medline, Cochrane CENTRAL, EMBASE, Outbreak Database, PsychINFO, and the Health Management Information Consortium database. The review included studies published between January 1, 1996, and December 31, 2012, with landmark papers published before 1996 also considered. Eligible studies were in English, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish, provided an English title or abstract was available. The SIGHT search was stratified by thematic areas, including organizational and structural arrangements for IPC programs, surveillance and outbreak management methods, education and training of healthcare workers, behavioral change interventions, and local policies for isolation precautions. The inclusion and exclusion criteria for the SIGHT review are detailed in the appendix of the main publication. Initial assessments involved screening titles and abstracts against inclusion/exclusion criteria, with a second reviewer assessing one-third of the titles and abstracts and all full texts. Disagreements were resolved by consensus or a third reviewer. The quality of studies was assessed using the Integrated Quality Criteria for Review of Multiple Study Designs (ICROMS) scoring system. Two reviewers conducted the quality assessment, resolving disagreements by consensus or consulting a third reviewer. Studies were graded as low, medium, or high quality based on the ICROMS summary score. An expert group reviewed the categorization and elements of key components, assessed their applicability across the European Union, and defined corresponding structural and process indicators. Overall evidence was graded as low, intermediate, or high based on the median value of contributing studies. An update of the SIGHT review was conducted between November 2015 and March 2016 by the WHO IPC Global Unit team, using a similar methodology. This update included studies published from January 1, 2013, to November 23, 2015. Databases searched included Medline, EMBASE, CINAHL, Cochrane CENTRAL, Outbreak Database, and the WHO Institutional Repository for Information Sharing. Articles in English, French, Spanish, and Portuguese were included if an English title or abstract was available. A comprehensive list of search terms, including Medical Subject Headings, was used. Inclusion and exclusion criteria were based on the evidence needed to answer the research question. The inventory of national and regional IPC action plans and strategic documents was developed to identify, record, and analyze documents addressing key IPC components. This approach covered all six WHO regions. Starting in October 2015, the scope of work was mapped out through meetings with the WHO Department of Pandemic and Epidemic Diseases/AMR team, the Infection Control and Publications Unit, and WHO regional focal points. These meetings examined IPC components being implemented or required across regions and countries to reduce HAIs and tackle antimicrobial resistance (AMR). The WHO Department of Pandemic and Epidemic Diseases/AMR team provided a repository of AMR national action plans/strategies, forming a solid starting point for sourcing documents. WHO regional focal points were asked to provide input on existing documents from countries and regional offices. A short survey was conducted via Datacol from January 20 to May 13, 2016, to retrieve existing IPC national programs and documents. All documents were reviewed in a two-stage approach: (1) content review targeting specific sections relevant to national and facility-level IPC, and (2) electronic keyword-finding to extract relevant information from Word or PDF files. The results of the systematic reviews and regional inventory were presented at a Guideline Development Group (GDG) meeting held from March 30 to April 1, 2016. The GDG formulated recommendations based on the quality of evidence, the balance between benefits and harms, values and preferences, resource implications, and feasibility. The strength of recommendations was rated as either strong or conditional. Full consensus was achieved for most recommendations, except for one related to core component 4b, where opinions varied. Areas requiring further research were also identified. In the absence of direct evidence, the GDG developed good practice statements to highlight essential IPC components. These statements were based on a compelling body of indirect evidence supporting the net benefit of the recommended actions.
